utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You intend to use English in giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you first of all make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by repeating the document which is about to be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. The situation is a bit different from the last time you were here. The Trial Chamber has the evidence that you gave before; it also has your statement. So we've got a lot of information. You're here so that counsel representing the parties, both the Prosecution and the Defence, can ask questions to increase our knowledge, if they can, either by supplementing the information you've already given, clarifying things, and in some instances, no doubt, challenging what you've said. To give us the maximum benefit of this hearing, it would be of great assistance if you were able to concentrate on each individual question that's asked, concentrate your answer on the point that the question is directed to. The first person to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And before I start may I introduce Mr. Michael Hehn, who is assisting me today. He's an intelligence analyst with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: My name is Baton Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I'm a journalist. For the moment, I am editor of the Express newspaper in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 20 August 2001?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in May 2002, did you sign a declaration, and did you give a short addendum statement at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. I made the addendum here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here this week to testify, did you have the opportunity to read your statement and the addendum?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did read it. It was the same, and I have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you went through your statement, did you point out one issue; namely, a date which is on page 3 of the English version, which refers to the following sentence I read it out: "For me the war in Kosovo began on October 1st, 1998, when the students held their first peaceful protest." Did you make a correction regarding this date?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. The correction is related to the year. It was the 1st of October, 1997, and not 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And including this correction, can you attest today that your statement and the addendum are true and correct, and that you would testify what is contained in these statements if you were examined on all these questions today?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I have nothing to add to what I've stated in my statement, and I will respond to every question you will make.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit P2478 at this stage; it's the 92 bis package of the witness, including statement and addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you also testify in the Milosevic trial on 23rd May 2002?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But it wasn't this room, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here this week, did you also have the opportunity to read the transcript of your testimony at that time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. I read it last night -- yesterday, as a matter of fact, the transcript and my statement, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you are quite fluent in English, are you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Relatively fluent. This is a language that journalists use a lot for communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And now after having read your -- the transcript of your testimony, do you also attest today that you would testify the same if you were examined about all these questions today, and that what you said then is true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. I've said the same things before, I've published the same things in the media, and I will say the same things today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit 2479 which I would like to tender now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhiu, I would like to go through some areas of your testimony and your statement, starting with what you stated about the education system in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this is page 3 of the statement, Your Honours, and in the transcript it's pages 5388 to 5393.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, you stated that in 1991, there was a change of the curriculum which also included that the Albanian language was no longer allowed as a language in the education system. Can you explain to these Honourable Judges why was this change of education so important for the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Before there was a gradation of problems until this decision was made. There was constitutional changes in 1989; and then the state of emergency later; and then the decision to change the educational system. A new curriculum was imposed, and this curriculum foresaw that all the Albanian students had to have their education in the Serb language, with the exception of the primary schools. So the Albanians were not only ex-communicated physically, so they were not allowed to enter the buildings of the schools in Kosova, but also it was imposed upon them to learn and study according to the Serb curriculum. And this triggered the crisis, together with firing en masse of the workers from their jobs. The contribution for the creation of this university was not made by the Serb state, but by the Kosovan citizens themselves. And this created the basis of the conflict which then led to a total war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And you already mentioned the creation of a parallel system, a parallel university, where I think you yourself also obtained your degree, your final degree, from. You mention in your statement that the diplomas of this parallel university were not acknowledged by Serbia. So what would these young people after graduating from this parallel university actually do? What opportunities would they have with this degree?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I have to clarify something here. The educational system was a total apartheid. For example, the primary school aged children were divided by walls, while the older students were not allowed to go into these buildings. In the beginning, we had these two alternatives; either to create a parallel system or to create conflict and enter into a war. A conflict would be suicide for Albanians, because we knew that the Serbs were very powerful. And the whole Army of Yugoslavia could be against Kosova at the time, as they were in Bosnia and Croatia. So we didn't want the situation to degenerate into a conflict. So that was the only possibility, the only alternative, to create this parallel system, to create an illusion that something would change, and to give everybody some time and hope that the situation would change for the better in the future, hoping that the Milosevic government would become aware of the situation and create some dialogue to come out of that situation. That's why that parallel system was an attempt to avoid war after 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now to come back to my actual question. Young people graduating from this parallel university, when the diplomas were not acknowledged by the Serbs, what were actually the opportunities that young people, young Kosovo Albanians, had at the time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were two alternatives. In the beginning there was only one, as a matter of fact, because the Serbian state did not recognise the diplomas. The only alternative was pack your bags and go to the west. The other one was the conflict and unpleasant situations because of the large presence of the police. Secondly, it was a very difficult situation at the time, because the Serbian state was asking young people to join the army. So the only possibility for those young people at the time from 1991 to 1995 was to enter this parallel system of education and then leave Kosova. So this was the first alternative. The second alternative was to get organised against this regime who had violated the dignity of each and every Albanian, breaking into their homes, into their work-places, and what had never happened with the earlier Serb regimes, they broke into people's homes until 1997 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, I do have to interrupt you, I'm afraid. Our case is principally concerned with 1998 and 1999. Background is important up to a point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but we can't possibly go into all this detail. You were asked a question about what opportunities were actually available for young graduates from the parallel system. And you've said one was to go to the west. Could you perhaps tell us if there were any other opportunities for them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other alternative was to go to the mountains and join the fledgling KLA, and what we can say about the situation is that the last attempt to avoid this situation was the education agreement signed by Milosevic and Rugova. This was the last attempt to stop the young people from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Prior to that agreement, though, which was in 1996, is it realistic to say that young Albanians were joining the fledgling KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Until the agreement, there was no fledgling KLA in Kosova; at least we did not know about any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Moeller's question's related to after 1996. She was asking you what the position was when the parallel system was set up and running. So the only option that it would appear you've identified was to leave Albania and go try to find work somewhere else -- to leave Kosovo, rather, and go to the west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you'll understand that it's taken a long while to get to this point, and it's important that we make maximum use of the limited time we do have. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, you already mentioned the San Egidio agreement, the education agreement of 1996, and this agreement contains the clause that Albanian teachers and pupils should return to the universities. Was that actually ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, it was not implemented. And the only institution that was allowed was the Albanological institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Then in October 1997 there were the student demonstration, as you state on page 3 of your statement, English version. Were these demonstrations announced beforehand?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, they were announced in the media and press conferences, the organisers had these press conferences, and also the rector of the university. What they said is that if these facilities are not available to Albanians, then the protests will start.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you stated that the police intervened violently. How many police intervened at this demonstration, roughly?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Let's say at the place of the event, about 500 to 700, but the whole town was full of policemen, every street, every junction, everywhere you could see policemen. But after the announcement of the organisers that this protest would take place, the policemen were positioned in the key points, and their intervention was brutal, very brutal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were there any vehicles involved in the police operation?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I am not an expert of those vehicles, but there was a vehicle with some kind of grid which was in front of the students. I was about 20 to 30 metres away from that place where the students were. And then there was a helicopter flying over the group of students, about a hundred to 150 metres high. I can't say exactly how high. And there were hundreds of policemen and lots of vehicles behind. The students did not give any signal that they would be violent in their demonstration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So what was this very brutal way of intervening, if you could describe that? What did the police do?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: First of all, the order was given to this vehicle to start -- this vehicle with a grid. And behind that there were policemen. At that moment all the students sat down, and this vehicle which was armoured came very close to the first group of the students, right up to their faces. And then the policemen who were wearing helmets intervened. There were some other people in plain clothes who intervened as well, and they began beating up the organisers. And then tear gas was used against the students. There were about 20.000 people there, and hundreds of tear gas bombs were used in a place which was very dangerous because it was a very narrow street. And I had never seen before such brutality on the part of the police, and that was a critical point of the Kosovan crisis, and from that time on everything precipitated for the worst.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you find out at any point who was responsible for this violence used by the police in this action?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I learned this later as a matter of fact, but in the meeting that I had with Jovica Stanisic, Bakalli, and myself, the name Lukic was mentioned and at that time I did not know who he was, but they said he was the chief of Drzavna Bezbednost, public security, chief of the public security. Before that time I had not heard about him. At the day when this happened, though, we did not know who had given this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is page 9 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the corrections you made when you did your addendum was to change a reference to the second student demonstration. The one we're talking about was on the 1st of October. When was what you describe as the second student demonstration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened approximately one month later, and the organisers were the same people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, so that date must be wrong as well then, because it's given as the 1st of November, 1998, but that should be 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The day or around the day of this student demonstration in October 1997, you state - this is page 4 of the statement - that the police also broke into the Koha Ditore office, and you state that they beat yourself and your colleagues a bit. Can you describe what the police officers did you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We returned to the offices after the event. Ten minutes after we entered the offices, a large group of policemen wearing helmets entered, and they broke the door in. They hit the director, Luan Dubroshi first, then they grabbed me by my throat and hit me. Then they went after the group of journalists who were recording the demonstration. Fatos Berisha, who was the cameraman, he jumped from the second floor and he broke his leg. He works today at the television centre and he still suffers from that leg now. Fortunately, Nicholas Hill was inside and he saw the event with his own eyes. He was there in the office. Nicholas Hill was from the American embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move on now. You also talk in your statement about the closing down of some Albanian newspapers and magazines in the early 1990s, specifically you talk about the police closing down Bota e Re in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, does this sort of thing justify examination in oral evidence, going back to the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I submit it does, Your Honour, because it's a huge part of the background that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know what the result will be, that the Defence will bring a very expansive case about the early 1990s and at the moment it's very difficult to see what the relevance is. This has implications for the whole trial. Now, what is the relevance of looking at the early 1990s when we're talking about in this indictment brutality in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, we set out quite concrete allegations in the background section of the indictment, including those, and I think as the witness states in his evidence. These discriminations that happened in the early 1990s played quite a role in the later events, and as we have them in the indictment as allegations in paragraphs I think 80 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- to 102, we live under the premises that we have to prove these allegations to some extent as well and he is one of the few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll be hear to the next century doing that in the Balkans, because there are 101 different views about virtually everything that happens there. We have to concentrate on what is significant in this trial. Now, you tell me what the relevance of the early 1990s and the closing down of the press was before we decide whether to listen to more of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As I've said, it is a part of the indictment, and so far we have been told to prove every aspect of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who has told you to prove every part of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a normal procedure in every legal system I would be familiar with, that you have to prove allegations you set out in an indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which paragraphs should I be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You should be looking at paragraph 88, which has the third sentence: "Throughout late 1990/1991 people were dismissed, local courts were abolished, judges removed." Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how did that contribute to the charges in the indictment in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I think it contributes to the -- to the overall building-up of a joint criminal enterprise, which came in force no later than 1998, but that means at the same time it may have come into force earlier, and there certainly was a build-up over years for this situation to erupt as it did then in 1998 and 1999. And this is why we included the background section into the indictment because we think it is -- it makes sense to have a certain background to the events and to -- the build-up of the situation to put you, as the Court, in a position to judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me the relevance, the direct relevance, of these events to what you allege the Serbs did to Albanians in 1999. Tell me the direct relevance, what it did -- what the picture, your theory of the picture is that this will amplify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, the picture is that what -- what erupted in 1999 was only the outcome of something that had started in the early 1990s, and the same politics that were applied already in the early 1990s also were part of the discrimination which again then was part of our case in 1999. This witness will also talk about what happened to his newspaper then on 24 March 1999, which was like the final measure taken against him and his newspaper, but before that happened for many years there were other forms of discrimination and other things which I think cannot be left out of the picture. It would be artificial. And generally I -- the reason why we included this background section into the indictment and why we lead evidence on this is that it has also been a common practice in this court to give some background in the cases of political and social --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The background's in the written statement. Give us a moment to consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't consider it appropriate to explore this any further in oral evidence. It's in the written material that we have in front of us. We have to concentrate on 1998 and 1999, and we'd be grateful if you would go to that period, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, where were you -- or let us first go to 1998. In the transcript you testified about going to Malisevo in May 1998. How was the situation in Malisevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was the only place that could be called a free place. It was controlled by the KLA. There were refugees there who had come from different parts of Kosova, mainly from Drenica. You could see houses overpopulated; on the other hand, you could see people anticipating an attack. You could see houses that had been burned along the Pristina-Peje road, and of course there was fear of attacks that would make the situation in Malisheve, which was controlled at that time by the KLA, even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How big a group of refugees did you see, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I can't say how many there were. There were people on the roads. There were people in the houses of this small town. Mainly this town was inhabited by refugees who had fled from Drenica, which had been attacked, and there was also people from the Dukagjini area, which had moved to that area after the well-known meeting of Milosevic with the Kosovar delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you go to any other areas in Kosovo between, let's say, June and October 1998?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We mainly travelled in the company of journalists from Reuters and Associated Press. I went there immediately after the offensive that was launched by the Serb forces on Rahovec. The entire population of Rahovec had moved to Berisha mountains, and this was the reason why we visited this area with two diplomats, David Slinn and Jan Kickert. And the aim was to convince the KLA to start a dialogue to give -- to put an end to the war, and to establish a provisional government that would, in a way, pave the way to dialogue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, can you assist me to find in the statement the reference to events at Malisevo in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is in the transcript, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is page 5429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many refugees are we talking who, as you said, fled to the Berisha mountains, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The three of us saw a horrifying situation. In the Berisha mountains in all that area I would say there were over 100.000 refugees. The number perhaps even didn't matter, but there were a lot. The situation was terrible. The representatives of the KLA asked the two diplomats to provide humanitarian aid for the refugees because the situation was really horrifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which other areas, if any, did you go to during this time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I personally went to this area, but Veton Surroi and Chris Hill went to -- Ledam Shala [phoen] went to the other area. They wanted to convince the KLA to start a dialogue to pave the way for this provisional government. The dialogue was very harsh in a way because of their convictions, but in a way this discussion came to an end. We could not see a single house that had not been set on fire along our road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And along which road would that be, if you can explain the road you referred to?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We entered a road that went to Lipjan, a small town near Pristina. That road went through small villages. Since I was not familiar with that area, I asked throughout the journey where the Berisha area was. Of course, there were policemen along the way, on the road Peje-Prishtine, on the left side. Along this road you could see houses that were burned. At least me, personally, I didn't see a single house that looked normal and undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in spring 1998, did you ever go to Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was in the newspaper offices, and from Julian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- informed us that there was an attack launched on Prekaze early in the morning. They told us which roads had been blocked. They asked us to go there and report on the incident. We -- I told him personally that the only way to get there was through the road that goes to Vushtrri, since he said that all other roads had been blocked. We got on a jeep, Land Rover. We took to this Vushtrri road that led to the village of Lipovec as far as I know, and approached the area of Prekaze village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to summarise it a bit more. We are short on time as the Presiding Judge already told us. Could you repeat who you went with. I think the second name was missed by the transcript. Julian was the first name. What was his last name?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Broadfight, Julian Broadfight, first secretary of the British Embassy. And Jonas was the first secretary at the Swedish embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did these two diplomats later report on Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They went on two days there. They reported on the incident, and afterwards they were proclaimed persona non grata. There was a report in Novostine [phoen] newspaper which contributed to them being persona non grata by Serbia, and they were later replaced by other diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we going to see the reports that these diplomats made?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because they are not witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a reason for that? This is the sort of, you know, independent material that obviously would be of use to the Tribunal in picking its way through the versions that we hear of events. Anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to move now to 1999. Shortly before the war started you were summoned to court and convicted for a publication that appeared in Koha Ditore, of which you were editor-in-chief at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, we published a communique issued by the General Staff of the KLA. This communique was also published by Bujku and other newspapers. To my recollection, it was a Friday. Afterwards, we were immediately summoned by the judge for a court session that was scheduled for Sunday at 3.00 p.m. We went there in the morning. The judge told us that you have published this and this article. In order to prolong the procedure, I said I did not speak Serbo-Croatian, although I did, and that I requested an interpreter. So they called us again on Sunday, and on this occasion they communicated the verdict to how -- to what I was sentenced. He said, the judge said, that this is not my fault. This was an order that I received from Belgrade. This was on the 22nd or the 23rd, I don't remember exactly the date, but it was two days before the bombing started. And my lawyer Bajram Kelmendi was informed. He was killed later on, together with his son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Two sons, correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did I rightly identify in your material whether the statement of the transcript, that that killing was very close to the time of your conviction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 24 or 48 hours later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't believe that his killing is related to what Mr. Kelmendi defended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you say you were summoned to court on a Sunday. Was it normal for courts in Serbia to sit on a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. I think this is a unique case in the entire world, for a session to be held on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're looking for extra time if we can get it, Mr. Haxhiu. It's an interesting possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, you said this article, that statement of the KLA was published in other papers. Were any other people, to your knowledge, convicted for having published it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no. He was not convicted, and not even summoned to court. Koha Ditore in fact was an object of pressure exercised by the police. They were aware of the fact that we would not respond to their calls unless they sent a written summons. They began to visit our offices and ask us questions about things that they had no right to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So let me ask you, before this trial and conviction on the 22nd March, there were other occasions on which Serb authorities tried to interfere with your newspaper, were there?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were other occasions, but I don't know of anyone being convicted except for an editor-in-chief who was convicted in Belgrade, a courageous one, and actually he resembled us at Koha Ditore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, just to put this in context and without commenting in any way about the rights or wrongs of what happened in this instance, on which it may be impossible for us to make a determination because we don't have the newspaper as far as I'm aware, but your paper was allowed to continue to operate, was it, or did this close you down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was closed down two days later. On the 24th, all the computers were confiscated. The entrance to the offices were blocked, and the print-house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I understand that. But was that in any way connected with the fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And thereafter, what was the future of Koha Ditore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was closed down because the bombing started. The police entered and the print-house was burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it resumed publication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It resumed publication in exile, in Tetovo, and later on, after we returned, it again resumed publication in Kosova, after 12th June 1999, when all Kosovars returned to Kosova. But during the relevant period that we're speaking about, the building was confiscated by the police, the computers, the entrance was blocked, and the printing house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: One more question relating to Koha Ditore. I understand from your statement that it was first a weekly magazine and only in 1997 became a daily political newspaper. Given the situation of the press and media situation in Kosovo at that time, how did Koha Ditore ever get permission actually to become a political daily newspaper?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was a pressure on the part of the western countries to allow the functioning of a newspaper in Kosova. Part of it was financed by George Soros. We functioned with a minimal budget, but we reached a maximum circulation. Why we turned it into a daily newspaper was because it wasn't possible through a weekly magazine to treat all the problems prevailing at Kosova at that time. Bujku was a daily newspaper that was sort of a compromise between the Serb government, the Democratic League of Kosova, and the international community --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. You mentioned Bujku. Why wasn't Bujku closed down when in the early 1990s many Kosovo Albanian and other newspapers were closed down, or taken over by the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The word itself, "Bujku," means that this is the newspaper dedicated to agriculture. The word itself means a farmer. Maybe the Serb government allowed it for cynical reasons. It is -- and by making it the only newspaper that was not closed down, they wanted in a way to show that there is a newspaper existing and that's how it remained. It served the Democratic League of Kosova. It was a big lie, this newspaper, as was the entire regime and the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on 24 March when the NATO campaign started, where were you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was in a Pristina neighbourhood called Bregu i Diellit. In the house of a friend of mine, who is a journalist and a writer, Teki Dervishi, we spent, if I can put it that way, half the time inside the apartment and half the time in the basement. When the bombing started, we thought that the war will come to an end soon, that the bombing will only last for three or four days, and that a solution, political solution, to the situation would be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the basement at this apartment?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I stayed there till the 29th, then I went to another location. On the 2nd, I left Kodra e Diellit together with hundreds of thousands of other refugees who were fleeing the town under the orders of soldiers or whatever they were who were showing us the road where to go and how to leave Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. These soldiers -- you say "under the orders of soldiers." Can you describe how -- I mean what kind of orders were these. Were people -- did people flee on their own flee will, or were they told to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. They had formed a line at the rear of the column. Some others were giving orders to houses, to people to leave their houses. The order was "napred," forward. It was a group of people who were rather fat because -- and I wouldn't say they were soldiers or policemen because the policemen and soldiers that we knew were elegant in a way so -- they were slim. They must have been paramilitaries or members of groups. In every street, there was a vehicle, military or police vehicle, and on every junction there were vehicles who were giving us directions. We reached the border, we remained there for a couple of days because the Macedonian government would not allow us to cross into Macedonia --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the soldiers -- you say they were fat. What kind of uniform, if any, did they wear? And if you could make your answer a little bit shorter, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I had never seen before such uniforms. It was green.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Plain green or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was camouflage, green with camouflage pattern. Some of them had overalls.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what do you understand to be a paramilitary? You mentioned that you think they were paramilitaries. How do you distinguish a paramilitary from the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Well, it's logical. You can distinguish them because of their weight, you can have a look at them and you see that they're different. And the way they were ordering people, it was not military language, it was very harsh language, typical paramilitary language. I don't know whether they were paramilitaries or not, but because of their bodies, the way they looked, and the language they used, I thought they were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that these men in the green camouflage uniform operated absolutely independently of the army and the police in Pristina? Because you mentioned that police and army vehicles were in every street -- or what do you mean by saying "paramilitary"? Because "paramilitary" may mean that this is an independent organisation in the military definition.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Well, if we speak about paramilitaries in Kosova, these were used as a group in May 1998 for the first time, and they were present all the time from that time on. And one of these groups were -- was headed by the chief criminal Arkan, whose base was in Grand Hotel in Pristina. We had information about this before, but for the first time we -- or, rather, I saw these people at Kodra e Diellit. I don't know anything about hierarchy or how the orders came from and things like that, but I -- that's all I can tell you about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you said you went to the Tetovo border. How was the situation at the border?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Horrible. It was a convoy of more than 15 kilometres. Thousands and thousands of people from Vushtrri, Mitrovica, Pristina, and all the villages along the way. Because Bllace, which was a place close to the border with Skopje, there was no room for anybody to stay there anymore. So the order was to go towards the border, and this was a kind of a pressure on the Macedonian government to allow these people to enter Macedonia. I was there for four days, but other people remained there longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haxhiu, can you explain a little more about the circumstances in which you came to leave Pristina. You were there in hiding for four days, and then could you explain how you came to come out of hiding and then leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was a publicly known person, I did not sleep at my house, as other people who are public persons. So we went from one part of the town to another. It was very dangerous to move during the night, so we tried to go from one place to another in the early morning, when there were not too many policemen in the street. At that time, I followed the news, the CNN and the BBC. We were thinking that the war would end in three or four days, but that did not happen. So a few days later we were all in these basements or houses which were not ours, houses of other families. In the morning of the 2nd of April, these forces dressed in green, as I said, came in that area and they had started expelling people from their houses. This was -- this had started in another part of Kodra e Diellit, but they were approaching us. Thousands of people had to leave their homes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the bit I'd like to clear up. What was it that made them leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What made them? Well, I think it was clear. It was ethnic cleansing of the area. They did not want Albanians to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what happened? What did people do or what was it -- just tell us the facts. Don't tell me that it was ethnic cleansing; that's something that we may have to decide eventually. Just tell me what was happening on the ground where you were that you say caused the people to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More concretely, this group of people in green uniforms, part of them was guarding the people who were down the road, while the other part of the group went from house to house and told the people to leave their homes. And that's how in two or three hours all the houses were abandoned by the people. All the people were told to leave their neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you actually see that happening, people going -- people in uniform going into houses and forcing the population to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it with my own eyes. I declared this, I stated this in the press conference I held in Bonn, then also in London and Paris. On the 8th and 11th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't need to know the whole history of how you've dealt with this since.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you notice anyone refusing to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was impossible to refuse. People were scared. There was a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if someone did refuse and what happened to them? I'm trying to get the facts, not generalisations about circumstances which don't help Judges to reach conclusions. In a court -- I'm sorry, I'm having to explain this to people at this stage, but in a court we work on facts, and I would like the facts that were occurring at that location at that time that caused people to leave. I think it's a simple matter but it doesn't seem to be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could you say no to people carrying guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See, that's a good start. That's the first mention of guns, I think. Let's get the facts. It's not for me to put words in your mouth. I want to know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think some things are self-explanatory because they were carrying guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean, "things are self-explanatory"? We weren't there. Fortunately we weren't there. We have to hear it from the people who were. I'm sorry about that, but we can't make assumptions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Then I will tell you that those soldiers were carrying guns and they wore masks and they went from house to house and ordered people to leave, each and every house. That's why there was this large group of people who were leaving their homes on the 2nd of April, and I was a witness to what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you see a good security reason for requiring people to leave their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Only the 24th and 25th there were news about people who had been killed, Bajram Kelmendi and others. So people were scared. So I cannot explain you from this far back in time. It was so long ago, and the fear at that time was extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've misunderstood my question. I'm trying to find out if there was some good reason, rather than bad or evil reason, why it would be necessary to move people from these houses. Was there something else happening that moving them from the houses would provide security to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I have to explain this. I cannot say everything in one sentence, but however I'll try. Every Albanian that was in Pristina at that time was metaphorically dead. They could not do anything to save their lives. We all ran the risk of being killed. You cannot even try to comprehend the situation that existed there at the time, two days before the bombing and two days after the bombing as well. Hundreds and hundreds of policemen were on the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not making myself clear. We've heard evidence in other circumstances of people being moved because it would be safer for them if they were somewhere else. What I'm trying to find out is whether there was some good reason why it might have been safer for the people in Pristina to be moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, fear is part of the human being and it is possible that some of the people were scared and wanted to leave from a place where killings were happening to Macedonia, where they would feel safer. So fleeing from death and going somewhere where you could have the hope of being alive, that was a satisfaction for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I cannot deny the fact that there were people who left because they were scared and they wanted to find a safe place to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to something else. In your -- the statement in 2001, you referred to your involvement in attempts at negotiation. And you say in the statement: "In the beginning of November 1997" you got a phone call from a man named Stijovic. Now, was that in fact November 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So attempts were being made instigated from the Serb side to engage Albanians in discussion in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, it was an attempt made by the Albanians, not the Serbs, but we wanted to have mediators from the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that this started when you were detained and there was a so-called conversation and that that detention was at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- was at the instance of Serb authorities. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm clear about the situation. Yes, this happened after I was called for the so-called informative talk, for questioning. It was about -- it was either the 2nd or the 3rd of October, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Moeller, perhaps you can help with something else. In these various corrections that were made in this addendum, one of them talks about sending a letter to various people. It starts with reference to Rugova. Where does that fit into the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If I understand it correctly, it -- it relates to after the meeting with the state security -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it's not clear to you, perhaps the witness can help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You at one stage sent a letter to various people, including Rugova, Fehmi Agani, and Hill, and others. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not like that. I only sent a letter to Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's my -- I have misread it. You're quite right. Now, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was after the meeting that occurred with Jovica Stanisic; it was mid-December. And we were trying -- after what happened with the students, we were trying to start this dialogue and not choose the path to war, because we saw what happened in Bosnia and Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in your statement. I'm just trying to get the complete picture and the order of events is important here. There then is reference to meeting Stanisic on a later occasion. Was that in November 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a misunderstanding. I only met Stanisic once, while a preliminary meeting to prepare these meetings happened in Mr. Bakalli's apartment. I think it was two of his deputies, Hadzic and Gajic. They were very fat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date on which you met Stanisic? Just roughly. I just need to know the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th of December. It was before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's another correction that needs to be made to the addendum which refers to these events as in 1998, but it didn't tie in -- I mean, 1997 makes sense in the light of your overall statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only met this person once in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the cross-examination by Milosevic you referred to meeting his security service people three times; once in Bakalli's home, once in Brezovica, and another time when "they took me and interrogated me." Now, is that a reference to the first occasion when you were taken in and this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 2nd or 3rd of October was the first time when they sent me this invitation for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you. Bear in mind I'm just trying to get the timing of everything into order. Well, I'm just -- finally back to the subject of the movement of people, just so that we have a fairly accurate picture, the transcript today indicated you saying at one stage that when you left -- this would be on about the 2nd of April, that you left with hundreds of thousands of people. Now, is that an accurate -- an accurate statement of the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say there were more than 100.000 in the group that I left with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will proceed in the following order: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Ojdanic. But I believe it's the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We still have seven minutes, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd appreciate to get started and at least get something in before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hello, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic and I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic in these proceedings. I hope to obtain your cooperation to make this cross-examination move as efficiently as possible. Therefore, I would just ask you to please pay close attention to my questions and then try to give me the most honest and concise answer possible as we do have time limitations, and we need to finish your testimony here today so that you can travel. Now, first of all, I have two questions regarding the statement that was taken in 2001 by the Office of the Prosecutor. The statement states that you were interviewed by Mr. Fred Abrahams of the Office of the Prosecutor. Did Mr. Abrahams represent himself to you as an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. Somebody else was with Fred Abrahams, and he introduced himself as -- as an investigator. I think his name was Jonathan Sutch, if I'm not mistaken. He was together with Fred Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did, in fact, Mr. Abrahams take an active role in questioning you for purposes of preparing the written statement?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He asked some questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now moving to the substance of your actual statement, you've just now clarified a few things for me. It would appear now that all -- that both of the meetings that you had with state security, both the one at Mr. Bakalli's home and the one at the villa in Brezovica both occurred in 1997 rather than 1998. We're clear on that. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: One was two or three weeks earlier than the other one. So the first one was the preliminary meeting where we prepared the meeting, and then the other one was in Brezovica with Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, with respect to these two meetings that you attended, the Serb participants at these meetings were comprised of members of the State Security Service, the RDB, exclusively. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In Bakalli's house, two people introduced themselves as deputies of Stanisic. Their names were Hadzic and Gajic. They were very fat, as I told you, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time you understood Mr. Stanisic to be the head of the RDB, is that correct, the Drzavne Bezbednosti arm?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, he was the chief. They told us that they were his deputies, so their chief was Jovica Stanisic. But if you would like to know, I interviewed 21 people who -- functionaries of this organisation and they told me that he was chief of that organisation in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was what I had asked you, so thank you for answering that. Now, if we could focus first on the initial meeting that you had at Mr. Bakalli's house. You mentioned an individual named Hadzic or Adzic. Have you since that time been able to determine who in fact this individual was?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you arrived for the second meeting with the Serb representatives and you indicated certain individuals in plain clothes asked you to accompany them to Brezovica, first of all did you recognise or did you -- was it made known to you that these plain-clothes individuals were state security personnel?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you and Mr. Bakalli leave voluntarily with them?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Of course. This was the last attempt to achieve peace, to create a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Great. Now, when you arrived at your final destination at Brezovica, the villa where you were taken to, was this villa well secured?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I only saw civilians dressed in very good coats. These were young men, and they looked like twins. They looked all the same way. They were outside, and then Jovica Stanisic welcomed us. I had created a completely idea in my mind about him, but he was a pleasant person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. These persons you said that were like twins, these civilians, did you in fact -- were you told that these were also DB, state security, personnel or did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did not say that. These were young men. They were standing so straight, vertically. I think they were guards or they were Stanisic's body-guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicate in your statement that Mr. Bakalli told you that he recognised this as being a government-owned villa. Did he, in fact, explain further that he thought that this was a state security-owned property?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was told that during communist times that was used by the then-communist government, and he knew that that was a government villa. He did not tell me that it was a state security building. I had never heard about that villa before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time that you were present, did you -- could you tell us -- did you form a belief that in fact all of the proceedings were being recorded in some fashion; and if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: During the first meeting at Bakalli's house, I was taking notes, writing down what was being said, while they, they were speaking without taking any notes, without showing interest in our suggestions. That's why I created this belief that in a way they were recording these discussions, but in fact I did not know whether the discussion was being recorded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm asking you to focus on the villa at Brezovica. Did you in fact have any indications that that discussion, the discussions that were being had there, were also being recorded by the members of the state security apparatus?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Considering the fact that they said they would report to Milosevic the following morning at 8.00, I believed that, yes, they did. But I wasn't scared. I had my position, my offer, which in realistic terms was not accepted, and the situation deteriorated and the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, we have to have a break now for 20 minutes or so. The usher will show you where you can wait during that break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that will be at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we left off, sir, talking about the meeting that you had at Mount Brezovica with Mr. Bakalli and several representatives of Serb state security agency. I'd like to, first of all, ask you -- we left off talking about your understanding that the proceedings were being memorialised or recorded in some way. Did you understand that all your discussions, including those on the terrace, were being recorded, and when you were on the terrace were all the other individuals, Stanisic, Gajic, Bakalli, and Stijovic, all present?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is that a yes to both of my questions? I asked a compound question. First on the -- whether the talks that were held on the terrace of the villa were being recorded and then we'll move on to the next part of the question. So is that a yes as well?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: As to your first question, I already answered that. I said that that was my belief because they didn't take any notes. And as for your second question my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, do you know, sir, that a Serbian paper, Evropa, on 12 January 2006 published a transcript of some of the discussions that were held at the villa in Mount Brezovica in 1997. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll move on. Now, first of all, as far as your personal interaction with Mr. Stanisic is concerned, from the statement I see that the gentleman you identify as Mr. Stijovic was also always present with you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. He was present and he was sitting next to Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Stijovic was actively following the conversation that you had with Mr. Stanisic at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stijovic was following only the part of the talks that dealt with the students' demonstrations and the intervention, but not the rest of the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So he just was there for that part of it. And just to be clear, you recognised Mr. Stijovic from before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He was a citizen of Pristina. He was a member of the socialist youth association in Pristina. He was a well-known figure in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the top of page 9 of your statement you describe how you asked Stanisic about the student protests in October, and now we're clear that this is October of 1997. And you told -- you told us today that he told you that someone named Lukic had been behind the police intervention. Did Mr. Stanisic mention the full name of this Mr. Lukic or did he perhaps use a nickname?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: My question was the following: Why did you intervene at the students' demonstration when you know the importance of this demonstration? And he said - and I'm quoting him - "We had a conflict." This is what Mr. Stanisic said. "We had a conflict with the people of public security." He did not mention Mr. Sreten Lukic. He said Mr. Lukic, who did not share our opinion, and he was in favour of intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we can be clear, today you testified that in fact this Mr. Lukic was described to you as being the chief of the public security department. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was this Mr. Lukic described by Mr. Stanisic at that time, in 1997, as being the chief of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, this part of the conversation was not that important. We didn't reach a consensus for important issues for our future. I brought up this issue only to point out that there was intervention. The essence of our conversation was not the intervention at these demonstrations. It was part of the talks that we held, and in this context he mentioned Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I have just a few more questions about Mr. Lukic and then I'll move on to another topic. Now, first of all, in your statement you state that at that time you had no idea whatsoever who Mr. Lukic was. Did you at any point in time determine the position held by Mr. Lukic in 1997, specifically November and October of 1997, the time when you had your discussions with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I heard of Mr. Lukic only when he was accused by The Hague Tribunal and when I saw his photograph. I did not hear of him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you actually did not hear of him in -- any time in 1998 or 1999. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was not preoccupied with individuals; rather, with the regime, and Milosevic represented that regime. Therefore, I was not interested in the names of his, Milosevic's, people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, sir. Are you aware of the fact or have you since become aware of the fact that during that time-period, October and November of 1997, Sreten Lukic was in fact not in any command from the -- was not in any command position relative to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, but in fact was just an assistant police chief in the local city level SUP in a part of Belgrade and was nowhere near Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I already told you what Stanisic told me. I do not know to which Lukic he referred. I know only that he mentioned Lukic and Javne Bezbednost, public security. If you ask me about this person, I really don't know who he is. I only told you what his statement was and who gave the order for the intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you also stated that this Lukic was the chief of public security. Are you aware of the fact that Mr. Sreten Lukic did not become the chief of public security until January of 2001, coincidentally a few months before you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I never said that Mr. Lukic was chief of public security. I only interpreted Stanisic's sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your testimony here today that you don't know for a fact that the individual mentioned by Mr. Stanisic was represented to be Sreten Lukic, the man sitting at these proceedings and named in the indictment of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I already stated that in my statement I only mentioned the last name Lukic. Later on it coincided with Sreten Lukic, but at that particular meeting the name Sreten Lukic did not come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, what does the published transcript in Evropa say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's completely devoid of any -- of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours are interested, we have it scanned in the system and we have disclosed it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm curious that it was raised and then nothing came of it, and I therefore was curious whether anything about this aspect of the conversation might have appeared in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn for a moment to the student protest that occurred in 1997. During -- you indicated that the protests were announced publicly. Do you know whether in fact these protests followed the public law that was in effect at the time, that all protests had to apply at the -- all planned protesters had to apply to the police and give them specific notice of the extent of the protest, where the protest was going to be located, and what types of -- what numbers of persons were expected for the protest? Do you know whether the organisers of the student protest indeed followed those prerequisites of the law?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This applies to a system where a law is abided by. At that time the system did not respect laws and regulations. It did not recognise any protest and did not recognise any appeal for protest. That's why the organisers found the only way to inform them about the root of the protesters only through the media. The Serb regime did not accept any offer for protest at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any simultaneous protests at the same location being staged by Serbian students on the same day, as the Albanian student protests in October of 1997?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Protests by Serb students? Well, there was no need for them to protest. They enjoyed maximum security. They had a secure future. In a sense of their representation in the state and state's care for every Serb individual and student, something that the Albanians -- Albanian individuals and students lacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you was there in fact a counter-protest on the same day, in the same location as the Albanian students' protest that you have described, a counter-protest staged by Serb students?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were no protests by Serb students.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the -- strike that. The police forces did not intervene at all in the second protest that was held some 15 days later in early November of 1997, did they?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They gave the protesters 40 minutes for the protests. The entire neighbourhood was encircled by the police, and once this deadline passed, the police went in the direction of the protesters and they abandoned the neighbourhood. We are speaking now of the protest that occurred on the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that protest you say that the police gave 40 minutes. They gave 40 minutes when the organisers of that protest came, followed the law, and advised the police of the protest, and applied for a permit for the protest. Isn't that correct? Something they hadn't done for the prior protest.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when they saw the development of the situation after the first protest, they behaved as they did during the second time. But unfortunately young students had already started to go to the mountains, and it was too late for a correction on their part. You have to take into consideration the political context. The political context of the 1st October is a question of peace or war. To me, the war began on the 1st of October, and everything that was done a month later was in vain because nobody believed any longer in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm almost done with the student protests and I can move on. I just now have found the statement I was looking for. Your statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor in August of 2001 does not simply state Mr. Lukic was behind breaking up the demonstrations. On page 9, the first full paragraph it specifically says: "Sreten Lukic had convinced Milosevic to break up the demonstrations with force. At the time I did not know who Sreten Lukic was." Since you have now testified that the name Sreten Lukic was not used by Mr. Stanisic, how did this name come to be inserted in your witness statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2001? Was it suggested by Mr. Abrahams or the other OTP investigator present?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I'm not a person who can be influenced that easy. It's a political context. It's about people who were accused by The Hague Tribunal. I did not know any other Lukic from public security except for Sreten Lukic, and that's why it was logical to mention the name Sreten Lukic. I think I'm very clear in my statement that -- regarding what was said during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, this is quite confusing for me. The indictment against Mr. Sreten Lukic came out two years after you gave your statement. So how could the indictment have been the basis for you inserting "Sreten Lukic" into your witness statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor in August of 2001? Please help me.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I abide by what I've already said. The name "Sreten" was inserted on the basis of the political context and on basis of what was confirmed later for a person who was part of the police. During the meeting with Stanisic the name "Sreten" was not mentioned; only "Lukic" was mentioned as a person who worked in public security and as a person who convinced Milosevic that intervention was necessary. This was all that was spoken about regarding the events of the 1st October during these talks that we had about the future of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I've exhausted that area and I would like to now move to what you testified about in 1998. During the time-period of 1998, specifically when you talked about visiting Malisevo and the Berisa mountains, on those occasions you served as a translator for several OSCE and western officials. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. But in fact I went there to listen to the opinion of the KLA in a time of crisis that dominated Kosova at that time, and I thought that the influence of the media could make the situation easier. It was an attempt to convince the KLA to start a protest --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a process that would lead to dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, just so we're on the same page, the officials I'm talking about are Jan Kickert, Albert Rohan, and Wolfgang Petritsch. Do you recall going first of all in July of 1998 and then also thereafter with some of these individuals and translating for them what the KLA fighters were saying?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You're talking about another meeting and I'm talking about quite another meeting. The meeting in July 1998 was a meeting between Petritsch, Kickert, and a KLA representative. Mr. Johan Petritsch [as interpreted] and Jan Kickert, they had gone to Malisheve to see the situation with the refugees in Malisheve. And on the way this meeting was held, and this meeting was not longer than 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the meeting I want to talk about for the moment. Now, isn't it correct, as you told the Office of the Prosecutor on November the 7th, 2006, in your proofing session, that in fact during this meeting you purposely mistranslated what the KLA members were saying to try and make a more reasonable version, to kind of tone down the extremist rhetoric of the KLA to make it palpable to the western officials that were present, including Mr. Petritsch and Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I thought these were empty words. This was something untranslatable, and since this was not like a regular meeting, I didn't want them to get the wrong impression about people in uniform. I didn't want to be part of something that I didn't like; that's why I mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you changed the truth of what these people were saying and toned it down?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. I refused for something that was accidental to become a rule and to get that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This meeting was not the only time that you mistranslated what members of the KLA wanted to tell western observers, is it? You also did that once more to Ambassador Petritsch, who even asked you why the translation -- why the translation was so much shorter than the original Albanian version of what had been said. Isn't that correct? Again, as you told the Office of the Prosecutor just the other day.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It refers to the same event. We are speaking about the same event. I never translated differently from what was said on another occasion.
