utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you only misrepresented the truth on one occasion. Is that correct? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I already told you that we are speaking about the same events. You have mixed up the events. During this meeting, it was Johan Petritsch and Jan Kickert that were present. We are not speaking of a different event here but about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So my question to you was: You only misrepresented the truth on this one occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move on to another question, Mr. Ivetic. You have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we want to talk about Rahovec/Orahovac in June 1998, specifically prior to June 1998, isn't it a fact and don't you have knowledge of the fact that the UCK/KLA engaged in a huge offensive in the city of Orahovac in July of 1998, just prior to you being in Malisevo and the Berisa hills, in which the UCK attacked and almost took over the police station, keeping it under fire and surrounded for two days before reinforcements could arrive, and in fact took over the health centre and other main buildings in Orahovac town itself?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This is your interpretation. I did not see them take over Rahovec. I know that the offensive took place and as a consequence of this offensive there were hundreds of thousands of refugees. The Serb regime and police knew exactly how many refugees were in Malisheve and what was the risk of intervention in Malisheve and Rahovec. And don't forget that during that intervention on the right side of the road Pristina-Peje, all the houses were burnt down; and on the other side, during this intervention, the entire population was sent to the mountains. We are speaking here of a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Haxhiu, that in July 1998 the KLA did not try to secure any part of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the KLA did not have the power to capture Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That could well be true, but did they try was the question you were being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot witness to that here because I was not present there. This was the interpretation of the police and the army at the time, but if they attempted to take Rahovec -- to take over Rahovec, that was a mistake because they knew how many refugees were there in Malisheve and they would be at risk. I think that was something that was staged. The KLA did not have the power to take over Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say that's an interpretation of the police. Let me ask you a question based upon what Mr. Fred Abrahams testified to here before this Tribunal that occurred in Orahovac at exactly the precise same moment. He says that the KLA kidnapped 80 Serb civilians at once as part of this offensive. Do you have knowledge of that, if in fact the UCK was not capable of undertaking such an action?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You have to ask Fred Abrahams about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I did. That's what he told me. Does that change your lay opinion as to whether the UCK in the area was capable of undertaking such an action?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I am convinced that the KLA was not able to capture a town; I am very sure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- now, at some point in time -- strike that. Let me just ask some questions - here we are - relating to Pristina. Now, you testified as to the offices of Koha Ditore being broken into, et cetera, on -- I believe you said the day of the NATO bombings. Just to be clear, you were not present to eye-witness what occurred at the offices of Koha Ditore on that day, were you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I'm glad you asked me. Our guard was killed that day inside the building by the police, and he was thrown outside in front of the gate of Koha Ditore. And I carry the guilt for his death because I ordered him to stay on duty there that night. I never thought that that crime would be committed, and there is no stronger evidence for that than the killing of that guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, sir. You were not present and therefore did not eye-witness any of the events at the offices of Koha Ditore on the 24th of March, 1999; you were in a separate part of town. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That's correct. But I told you that the guard was killed and there is no stronger evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you left -- that you left with these other refugees that left. Now, what specifically were you told that made you leave that day?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was not told anything personally. I was amongst thousands of people who left at the order of those people in green clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you just a couple more questions about this event, and in particular these people in green clothes. Did you in fact see any emblems or insignia on these uniforms that these people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. The only thing I could distinguish them by was the local Serb language they used, the Kosovar Serb language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Great. Now I'd like to ask you another question relating to this. Is it correct, as you told the Office of the Prosecutor during your proofing session of November the 7th, 2006, that on that day when you were out on the street with these men in green uniforms, you did not see any persons in blue police uniforms on that day interacting with these individuals in the green uniforms. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They were not present in the act of expulsion, but they were positioned at every junction. So they were preventing the entrance of people and people getting out. So they were participants, because they were guarding the junctions. But, however, as I told you, the expulsion was carried out by the people in green clothes, in green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say the police were at junctions. Did any -- did you approach any of these police to speak with them and did they tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I like your cynicism. How can you imagine I could go and approach someone who wants to kill you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None of these individuals said that they were going to kill you, did they?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: These things don't need to be said; they can be seen. The armoured vehicles, the arms, the guns, the masks, and the helmet speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that time there was a war going on with NATO aircraft bombing Pristina every day, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's my turn. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Haxhiu. My name is Djuro Cepic, and I'm one of the lawyers representing Mr. Lazarevic. I would like to ask you a few questions. Mr. Haxhiu, you're from Pristina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you know where the OTP office in Pristina is located; I mean you know that it's there, right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You mean the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- no, I mean the Prosecutor's -- the office of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY, do you know where it is located in Pristina? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Pristina, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's where you gave your statement on the 20th, 21st, and 22nd of August, 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Part of the first statement was given at my home; the other one was given in Koha Ditore. And that time, in fact, I only confirmed that the statement was correct. I was interviewed at home and at the offices of Koha Ditore, and in fact there I only read what I had said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you signed the statement and you accepted it as your statement in its entirety. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. Because I wanted to see it in a written form because in -- the interview was carried out orally and recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 22nd of May, 2002, you provided an addendum to the statement, that would be one day before you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You signed it and you accepted it as your statement in its entirety. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, in all those documents, you never mentioned that you had been expelled. You never mentioned that the expulsion had been carried out by paramilitaries wearing green uniforms, yet here you are telling us all this today. Mr. Haxhiu, why did you change your testimony today? Did anyone persuade you that you should make a statement that is different to what you said in other statements? Let me just read what it says in the addendum -- page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I don't think it is proper to hold to the witness that he changes his testimony; he just added to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis for suggesting a change in testimony, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to read an excerpt from the addendum, paragraph 3, page 2, it's in English where it says: "[In English] ... on the 2nd April 1999 and went to Macedonia, where I continued to publish Koha Ditore. During April after I had left Kosovo," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. [Interpretation] So he never mentioned the expulsion, he never mentioned who actually performed the expulsion; he merely says he left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can ask that question, why he did not mention the expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm asking, Your Honour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different question from saying: Why did you change your testimony, which is what was objected to and I would sustain the objection to that. That doesn't -- isn't an accurate characterisation of the evidence. But to ask him the question that you've now asked is perfectly okay, why did he not mention the expulsion, so you can ask that question, but it's an entirely different question from the one you were trying to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I saw the distinction between the words "left" and "was expelled." So in the addendum it is stated explicitly that he left Kosovo, yet today he's saying that he was expelled. But I thank you very much for your correction and your instruction as to how to word my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Haxhiu, could you please answer my question. Why this change in your testimony -- your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's my mistake --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness is now capable of answering the correct question. Carry on, please, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for this semantic mistake that I made. I am saying now that I did not leave but I was expelled. I thought that would be self-explanatory. If I leave with 100.000 other people, this was not out of our own will. We were expelled. And if I made this mistake, I correct it now. We were expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, the statement doesn't mention 100.000 people either, so that really doesn't explain it. Are you able to say why you didn't go into the detail of leaving -- of the circumstances in which you left Kosovo when you were giving these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to tell you the truth, The Hague Tribunal investigators did not ask me. Well, yesterday while talking with members of the Prosecution, I explained it in -- just in passing, just by accident. That's why it appears in the statement. This part of the statement was entered into the statement after I met the members of the Prosecution yesterday. I'm not denying anything that I said in the previous statement; it's just that both are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I still have my habits from my judicial system, but at any rate I will now continue my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This figure that you mentioned, the 100.000 people, you mentioned it on page 5429 you described the -- your stay at the mountain near Malisevo in May 1998, yet in the trial of Mr. Milosevic and in the statements you never mentioned any refugees and let alone the figure of 100.000 people. So again, the same question: Is this again a grammatical, or rather, a semantic error or is it something else perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was not asked then. And today I was asked and I told you what the situation was like. While I testified here in the Milosevic trial, he did not ask me these questions. And when the Prosecution asked me today, I explained what the situation was. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in all those years, for well now seven years, you lived in Pristina, you know where the Office of the Prosecutor's office is located, and you never thought that it would be good to go there, and you never make this correction and you wait until today to present some new facts and new details that you have never ever mentioned before. So this what you're trying to say now, is this your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I object again to the word "correction," because it's additions but it does not corrections in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, this is an unproductive furrow that you're ploughing at the moment. The investigation of these matters is in the hands of the Prosecution. I don't think in a situation like this it's for us to be investigating the circumstances in which information of this nature emerges in the course of the investigation. There will be circumstances where that is appropriate, but not here. I think you should move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've actually completed my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's my turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhiu, just a few questions. In 1999, you were the editor-in-chief of Koha Ditore?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in light of this function you are familiar with the information act of the Republic of Serbia passed in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, because it came by post to our office and all the other newspapers offices, but I thought it was the worst possible media act. [In English] We have a man who did this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. We don't have a microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, let's confine the comments in court to the examiner and the witness, and if there is a formal intervention to be made, then please draw my attention to that by switching on the microphone. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, you remember that even in Serbia that act was criticised in public precisely because of the fact that it envisaged some Draconian punishment, forms of punishment, and provided very short deadlines for the proceedings before courts and for the actual enforcement of fines. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. There was only one case, the case of the chief editor of Blits newspaper. He was also convicted and then eliminated. But this happened to Koha Ditore as well. There was only a procedure that occurred in two days only. This happened to me personally as well with Koha Ditore. But you know who am I talking about, of course, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know. [Interpretation] I actually wanted to ask you: Do you recall that in accordance with this act, the information act, the investigating judge or, in fact, the misdemeanour judge was duty-bound to make the decision on any violations of the law within 24 hours? So within 24 hours of the publication of the information that was deemed to be in violation of it.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: And you think they could do this on a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I merely asked you whether you remember that the deadline for the ruling by the misdemeanour judge was just 24 hours, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was convicted on a Sunday, but what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the deadline for the enforcement of the fine imposed by the judge was, again, just 24 hours from the date of the ruling?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did not have time to do that because the bombing started. We had the decision to pay the fine or otherwise the newspaper would be closed down and I would be imprisoned, but there was no time to do that because the bombing started. We had 48 hours at disposal, as distinguished by -- from other cases that had only 24 hours to do that. But there have been only two cases, one in Belgrade and one in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you obviously have privileged status here. Do you know that the law envisaged that if the fine is not paid within 24 hours that it would be collected in -- by confiscating property and so on?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did not have time to think about that. The bombing started. It -- tragic and comic at the same time as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Whenever there's a cut-off date for a certain thing and a holiday intervenes, automatically the thing will go on the other day, that is the law perhaps in a civilised world, not a 24 hours are to be interpreted that way if it's a holiday, I mean because this is being confused and we are listening to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Your Honour. I can give you an explanation. I don't know if I can solicit that from the witness at this point. I'm just asking if he remembers that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, maybe you can assist us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in explaining whether criminal proceedings at that time would normally take place on a Sunday in any part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, according to the law on misdemeanours, there was a duty judge who was at all times on duty. So therefore, it didn't matter if it was Saturday, Sunday, or any -- or public holiday, whatever. So you had a duty judge for the misdemeanours, in the misdemeanours court. So therefore, this is not the part of the criminal law. This is actually a part of the law on informations. The informations act had within itself a certain criminal provisions and the fines which are to be imposed on the -- on the newspapers or editors-in-chief who were not obliged by the actual law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of another type of misdemeanour for which action would be taken so expeditiously?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whichever kind of break of the laws on public order, for example, if somebody would break the window in the middle of the night, I don't know, of a shop, not stealing anything, which would be a criminal offence, but something like that or, I don't know, start to demonstrate -- demonstrating in some way. That would be -- that would be considered as a misdemeanour and then he would be taken to the duty judge by the police. That's the -- that's the rules of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the football games. I mean, my learned colleague Mr. Fila is giving a perfect example. The football games, the football hooligans, that would be the kind of the situation, which usually happens on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you consider this to be evidence we would like to see some proof on that because we don't understand the law on information necessarily like that and it's not what the witness said. I understand him saying that there was a full trial on the Sunday, which is quite different from bringing someone in front of the duty judge, something we also have in my system, but this is not the same as a trial which is followed by a conviction next day. And if the Defence claims that this was a normal procedure, then I would like to see some evidence on that, if you consider what Mr. Zecevic said evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I am not treating this as evidence at the moment. I'm looking for guidance on the situation to help us investigate it, but it seems to me it's the duty of the Prosecution to prove that this was not normal practice. It's not for the Defence to prove that it was normal practice. The onus of proof is on the Prosecution here, so it's matter for you. But all we have is the witness saying what happened to him at the moment, which sounds unusual, but you would have to prove that it was contrary to law, I think. Anyway, carry on, please, with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhiu, I have just one question related to this issue. You reminded me of a case of the editor-in-chief of the Blits magazine. Do you maybe recall the case of Dnevni Telegraf paper?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, I meant Dnevni Telegraf and not Blits. I need to make that correction. Well, I meant -- yes. What I meant was Dnevni Telegraf and not Blits. Blits had just started to be published at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Dnevni Telegraf was a Belgrade daily. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was a very courageous newspaper. [In English] With the courage people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to correct one thing on the transcript, before it moves out of sight, on page 60, line 14,. I should have said if I didn't that it's not for the Defence to prove that it was normal practice. The word "not" should not be there. Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it not true that Dnevni Telegraph was a Belgrade daily, published in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Those who were against Milosevic and his regime, it's not important whether they were Serb or Albanians. Dnevni Telegraf, to tell you the truth, was a very courageous newspaper that had very courageous journalists. I don't understand your question. If you want to divide Albanians from Serbs, both people who were against Milosevic, then you can do that. But what I can say here is that there were courageous people at the time, both Serb and Albanian, and there are courageous people now. I don't understand the thrust of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It appears that there has been a misunderstanding. All I asked you is whether you know that Dnevni Telegraf was a Belgrade daily, that their offices were in Belgrade. I just asked you whether you know that, yes or no. I did not intend to make any distinction between anyone. This was just a very, very simple question.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I know Belgrade, I know where the offices are, and I know what is this about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, I think it was page 20, lines 3 to 5, you spoke about this when you said that you had known about a case in Belgrade and that it had involved some courageous people. I assume that you were talking about this very case, and you say that this was in fact almost identical to what happened to Koha Ditore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: What happened to Dnevni Telegraf happened just a few days before it happened to Koha Ditore. It was only a few days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. And their property was confiscated in precisely the same way because they failed to pay the fine within 24 hours of receiving the ruling. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That is not correct. The procedure lasted for a couple of days. There was appeals, but the confiscation started a week later, 10 to 12 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm representing Nikola Sainovic, and my name is Toma Fila. And just to help clarify this issue. We both know that the regular court was in Pristina, where the district court was, where the Supreme Court was. You were taken before the misdemeanour judge, and our mutual friend --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- defended you there. Is that correct? Bajram Kelmendi. I know that you -- he was your friend, Mr. Surroi's friend, my friend, and my father's friend. He was a good man.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Can I take this off, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, it will be easier for the two of us to communicate this way. So Bajram defended you before a misdemeanour judge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the questions about Sun -- the court sitting on Sunday, we can both agree that a regular court does not sit on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this -- I will agree with you that the law under which you were punished was not worth anything at all. I think we can all agree on --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to another topic. As a journalist, you know that in the Grand Hotel in Pristina in 1998, and I believe also in 1999, all the way up to the war there had been some kind of a media centre because press conferences were held there and all that, foreign reporters would go there, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the difficulties we're going to encounter here is the rapidity of the responses. There needs to be a time lapse between the end of the question and the beginning of the answer, where you're both speaking in the same -- well, you're not speaking the same language, but where you're listening, albeit responding in your own language, you're not waiting for the interpretation. So you need to bear in mind that you have to pause. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We know that the media centre was there. Are you sure you were able to see Arkan among the journalists there? Trust me, he was in Belgrade, a picture of him in the Hyatt was taken at the time.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Arkan had made reservations in the entire flat of the hotel, and we did see Arkan at Grand Hotel, unfortunately. His arrogance could be seen, was obvious, and especially in 1998 he was present in the Grand Hotel on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The 1998? You talked about staff.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I didn't talk about staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. We wanted to know whether he had some kind of staff and troops there. We all know what sort of person he was. I guess we understand each other. We were not talking about any type of staff. It doesn't suffice that you nod. You need to answer verbally. There was a misunderstanding. There was no HQ organised by Arkan at the Grand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There was a presence of Arkan and his people in the Grand Hotel. Whatever you call them. A terrorist group, criminals, I don't know how you would call them, but they were present there and his presence was very transparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I guess that's your answer. I can't do anything about it. But I would like to ask you something else. You are obviously friends with Mr. Surroi. You cooperated and so on. During your testimony --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We worked for 12 years together.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In his testimony, Mr. Surroi said that he participated in the talks, negotiations, whatever term we use, organised by the Bertelsmann Foundation. Before I move on to something else, I wanted to ask you this: At a certain point in your statement you say that you knew that Fehmi Agani was conducting some sort of negotiations and that Dusan Mihajlovic participated as well and his party deputy, Mr. Ratomir Tanic. This is what is in your statement. Is that correct, in your statement from 2001?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I did not mention him as a deputy. I only mentioned Ratomir Tanic. For a moment, he indeed was deputy of Dusan Tanic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says deputy in the statement.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us not dwell on this. It's important that we understand each other. I wanted to point out one part of the statement to you. Mr. Surroi, when talking about Ratomir Tanic, when he mentioned that very same Ratomir Tanic, said that he was Mihajlovic's advisor, albeit it is unimportant, and he said Tanic said that he had direct links to Milosevic but I didn't trust him. I always was distrustful of Tanic. Since you were friends, can you tell us why he didn't trust him? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Myself and Shkelzen Maliqi met him, Mr. Tanic, at a conference in Ohrid and we had the same impression, that he was very close to Milosevic, that he visits him. The ease with which he was telling things, discussing issues about dialogue, the reality was not that easy, the way he represented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps you didn't understand me because of the language I use. Mr. Surroi said I was always and I have always been distrustful of Tanic. I didn't trust him. Why did he say that? Do you know anything about that? What led him to gain that impression? Since you know you met the man as well.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You're speaking here of two people, myself and Surroi, that had much more important meetings than the meetings with Mr. Tanic. He is a marginal person as far as we are concerned, but sometimes even these marginal persons can be important in certain processes. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's switch to Serbian. Perhaps it will work better. Surroi said he didn't trust him and that he was always distrustful of him. Veton said that he didn't trust Tanic and that he was always distrustful of Tanic. Since you've been friends for 12 years, can you help us, why did he say that? Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I told you that we were public figures, and being public figures, we knew many people who were far more powerful and stronger than him, both politically and in terms of intelligence. Tanic was -- well, a man who overdid things. He spoke of serious matters in too far a light way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, he did not give away the impression of a serious person, although he wanted to appear as one. Is that so? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I already answered that, and I seriously don't know why Tanic is here in this question, why he's part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be clear to you, as long as it's clear to me. Just a moment to re-organise my thoughts. Oh, yes, another thing. It's not Tanic anymore. In your addendum, 1987 and 1988 always appear to be a problem. You were quite lucky that you mentioned 1988 and not 1987, otherwise you would have been cross-examined for two days. I apologise, 1997 and 1998. You told the Prosecutor why you participated in negotiations involving Stijovic, Stanisic, et cetera. I wanted to know something else. You said that you may have been the best-informed person in Kosovo, that you conducted 21 interviews with Serb politicians, all of which were highly positioned. And you said that you never interviewed Milosevic or his wife, but I don't understand this -- but I also did not interview anyone from the socialist party, Socialist Democratic Party, did you mean Korac? They have one member I think.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which social democratic party is it that you didn't interview any single politician of theirs? Did you have the SPS in mind? Do you want your statement?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I meant the party of Mrs. Milosevic. That is that I did not interview anyone from Mrs. Milosevic's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now it makes sense. You continue by saying that all of the politicians you interviewed said that Serbia controls Kosovo through its police and that only Milosevic and Stanisic can decide on the fate of Kosovo. What year was that? Did you have in mind any particular year or generally speaking? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: These are all public matters. The interviews date back in 1994, 1995, 1996, and 1997. After 1997, I did not have the opportunity to interview Serb officials any longer. To my recollection, the last interview I made was in June 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you organised a meeting in Belgrade together with Beta, you organised an internet service I think. Were you still under the same impression? You could hear the opinions from Belgrade via the Internet.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In order to stop the war, we created a site. We started with academic Cosic and another academician from Pristina. Our impression was that Milosevic was a person who decides over Kosova. Academician Markovic from the socialist party, when I interviewed him, he said that there were two persons who decide over Kosova, it's Milosevic and Stanisic, and not to mention Predrag Simic and other persons that I interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot Surroi, but I'm -- I forgot to ask Surroi, but now I'm asking you: Why did you not -- why did you not go out and have an election instead of going into a war?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, we didn't want to become part of a regime that was impossible to be toppled down through Albanians; and secondly, the -- there was no cohabitation between Albanians and Serbians. All the chances were given and lost. In 1997, Stanisic said that around Milosevic there are structural nationalists, nationalists that will never recognise Kosova as a republic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Sepenuk, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have them after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, except I'm going to guess I've got about three minutes. Before the break, after the break, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have them after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to break again now for half an hour, Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I won't go into the details of why we must do it. I think everyone here knows that I would be the first not to break if the opportunity was there, but it is not available to me I'm afraid. If your concern is if you will be finished today, I think it's pretty clear your evidence will be finished today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible to not break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's not possible, so please leave with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic, and I have just a few questions for you. As I understand it, you left Kosovo on April 2nd, 1999, and you went to Macedonia where you continued to publish Koha Ditore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you reached Tetovo in Macedonia on April 7th, 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: On the 7th of April at about 3.30 or 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right and how long did you stay in Macedonia, for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: From the 7th of April to the 26th of June. However, I entered Kosovo for the first time on the 15th of June. The rest of the days I used to transfer the office from Tetovo to Pristina. I commuted between the two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it fair to say that when you were in Macedonia during that period, you followed the war in Kosovo closely?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Well, as closely as I could because I was not present there. But we followed very closely every statement, every piece of writing, every interview that was given with relation to Kosova and on Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. I understand. And you say you speak English quite well. You're comfortable with the English language. I'll use an American expression now, rooting for somebody, when you're rooting like for a football team, you're hoping they're going to win. Do you understand that expression, when you're rooting for something or someone? You have to say yes or no. Do you understand that expression?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [In English] I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And is it fair to say that you were rooting for the success of the NATO air operation?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've also stated this publicly. I won't deny it, and I was convinced that NATO would win.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And you were so enthused about the NATO bombing that you actually, as I understand it, right before the war started you wore a shirt, probably a T-shirt, which said "NATO, just do it." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. And I placed that on the front page of my newspaper in October 1998 because the atmosphere was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I understand. And were you in touch with the various KLA commanders in the field concerning their role in guiding the NATO bombing attack?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. I didn't think they were prepared enough to give information to NATO with regard to NATO bombing. Part of the people who had joined the KLA were idealists and they did not know much about military affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were you discussing that with KLA commanders during the time you were in Macedonia by satellite telephone, for example?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I never spoke by satellite telephone when I was in Macedonia. Once I met in Tetovo Mr. Thaqi. It was the 12th or the 13th of June, 1999; that is after the Kumanova agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you know a person by the name of Timothy Garton Ash?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He's a friend of mine. He's a fellow journalist, and he's one of my favourite writers and journalists. One of the best writers in journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And he's written extensively on Kosovo affairs, has he not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Both during the conflict and before and after the war. He was dedicated to the Balkan conflict, especially the Kosova conflict, together with Michael Ignatieff and Kuchov [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as further -- as a further indication of what a good and respectable journalist he is, is it fair to say that he would rely at least in part sometimes on your opinion and he would interview about your views on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It could be said that. You could say that. He has spoken to me two or three times about Kosova, and a couple of his writings, one of them was a New York review book, where he cites me. He also cited me in other writings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And while we're on that subject, let me ask you about that article in the New York Review of Books which is called "Kosovo and Beyond" by Timothy Garton Ash, and it's 3D382.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, it's not Kosova and weapons -- oh, yes, "Kosova and Beyond."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you remember that article?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was that a good article, do you recall, accurate?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Timothy Garton Ash is known for being very accurate, but also he's known for his very clear opinions which sometimes are not based on information but on perception, because journalists have their own perceptions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- you mentioned that he's known for being accurate. Let me just read to you and you can follow along in the English, the first paragraph of this article. It says: "I'll tell you the truth," and that's in quotes, "says the Kosovar newspaper editor." "They really don't know. We are sitting in Tetovo Macedonia in the Cafe Arbi where the exiled intellectuals of Pristina meet the world. 'They' are not the intellectuals but the KLA commanders still in Kosovo, to whom the editor Baton Haxhiu talks daily by satellite phone. Besieged on their hilltops they can see a burning village here, a Serb patrol there, a tank at the crossroads, but they have no overall picture, yet a large proportion of NATO's bombing targets in Kosovo come from this same source, from the KLA commanders via satellite phone. So 'they' is also NATO." Is that accurate, Mr. Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: When you look at this sentence when it says "talks daily," or "talked daily," this does not refer to me, that I was talking to them every day. This is about the KLA people who had satellite telephone contacts in various ways of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Are you quarrelling with the use of the word "daily," or are you claiming that you didn't talk to them at all?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I received two phone calls by satellite, but I did not speak about my opinion, my opinion to I gave to Deutsche Welle and New York Times, that I felt humiliated that there was no one to protect me during my expulsion. So that KLA that had built some kind of reputation at the time was not there to protect me from my expulsion from Kosova to Macedonia. So that's -- on that occasion I received two phone calls which were semi-threatening, but they were not about anything that had to do with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: As I said, I was speaking about the KLA not being able to protect me from the Serbian army and paramilitaries. This statement was given on the 7th of April when I arrived in Tetovo, and I gave that to Deutsche Welle and New York Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But my question is more simple. I want to know whether you had any conversations. You say you didn't have them daily. Did you have any conversations with KLA commanders in the field about NATO bombings and the location of targets for the KLA by NATO. In other words, are you denying the accuracy of what your friend, Mr. Ash, has said in this article?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I said simply and clearly, I never spoke with them about NATO targets, absolutely not, because there was nothing I could tell them and I never spoke with KLA people about these things. I never spoke to any KLA commander about targets, because people from the international community were based in Tetovo and we had meetings with them, very frequent meetings, I would say. They wanted our opinion about the end of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you had no -- your testimony is that you didn't talk to KLA commanders and you had no knowledge while you were in Macedonia of whether KLA commanders or even members of the KLA helped NATO in determining bombing targets. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I'm reiterating the same again, and this is very accurate, that I never spoke to KLA people about targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So -- so Mr. Ash, your friend and who you say is known for his accuracy, got this one wrong? Is that plain and simple the case, he got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [In English] Better to say misquoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He misquoted you. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just to stay on this point that my learned colleague Mr. Sepenuk discussed with you, you said that you got two semi-threatening phone calls via the satellite phone. It wasn't really clear to me on the transcript who was threatening you and why. Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could not be taken as a full threat, but they were indignant that I had stated in Deutsche Welle and New York Times that nobody was there to protect me. My statement was about the KLA. All the people who were expelled had no protection from anybody; this was the essence of that criticism that I made. And if you could call that a threat, I received two phone calls that told me this was a mistake, and we did not have the power to protect you, that's why you were not protected. The fact that the KLA had gained this fame of being very strong was broken at the time when thousands of people left the country and nobody protected them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were there actually other occasions on which you were quite critical towards the KLA and what they did?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Many times, and sometimes my criticisms were very harsh. I took the courage to criticise them about things that I considered unpleasant, especially with regard to the creation of a government which would make it possible to create a new spirit, a new dialogue for overcoming this situation. I was with Jan Kickert and David Slinn in the Berisha mountains and at that time, on that occasion I had this very fiery dialogue with members of the KLA, representatives of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were you also critical of the KLA in some publications?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In what meaning?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In your newspaper, did you write critically about actions of the KLA or crimes committed by them?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We did not speak about crimes because they did not have the opportunity to commit any crimes, but we criticised them for leaving the places, their positions, and leaving the population at the mercy of the Serb forces. We criticised them for the way they were fighting and we criticised the symbols they used in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now to go back to an issue that was raised by my learned colleague Mr. Ivetic. The second student protest on 30 October 1997, it was discussed that no violence was used against the students at that time by the police. Was there any violence used against any other people that were present during this demonstration and did you actually help some victims of this violence yourself?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's very interesting, because that day that they did not use violence against the students they used violence in town. They changed tactics. They beat up some journalists. One of them, Ibrahim Osmani, was beaten up very badly. A journalist of Voice of America was also beaten up, and we took these people to a local private hospital because the state hospitals were controlled by the Serbs. That day was critical in town, but it was a calm day as far as the demonstration was concerned. -. However, I have to clarify one thing here. If the Serb police was applying the law that no notification had been made about this demonstration, the same police intervened the first time. So there was this legal ambiguity. This is what distinguishes a state where law and order reigns and other states where law and order goes amiss.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said "we" took some people to private hospital. Who was with you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We did not dare to transport them in our own vehicles. We used a diplomatic vehicle, a Land Rover, a blue one, it belonged to Julian Broadfight. We asked him to help us carry these people to a private hospital; they were in a very grave state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And now my last question relating to an issue also raised by Mr. Ivetic. The looting and destruction of the premises of Koha Ditore on or after 24 March 1999, according to your testimony you were in an apartment or basement hiding, and you confirmed that you did not see that with your own eyes, so who did tell you what happened to the premises of your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The next day -- I have to clarify something here. We did not know what war would mean, so we decided to go to the offices the next morning. So the next morning several journalists went to the offices and saw the guard who had been killed right at the gate of the building. There was no reason why to kill that person and put them right there on the step, on the doorstep, of the building, put him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I told Mr. Surroi that the guard was killed. And as I told you, I carried this guilt with me because I told him to stay there and keep guard on the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but the next morning, which day do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was the 25th, 9.15 a.m. when I received the phone call. The phones worked that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And you received the phone call from this colleague of yours who went to work basically and then found out that the place had been devastated?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you also stated in your statement that your flat was looted. Did you see that yourself or who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In my apartment at the time where my mother and my father and the police came, they took my -- a photograph of mine. That was a photograph that was taken of me in Racak with the bodies that had been killed. And they also had taken all the floppy disks and some other materials. And also a photograph of me with my son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were your parents there when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. My parents were there. They were told to go into one room. They searched the place --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So it was them who told you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: My father. And this happened later after I went to Macedonia. It was around the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Haxhiu, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to inquire regarding the Defence exhibits whether the Defence intends to tender Exhibit 6D108, which is the purported shorthand recording in the Evropa newspaper of the meeting between Mr. Bakalli and Mr. Stanisic, because we would object to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't moved for its admission and I'm not moving now either so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's not been tendered. The number's never been -- or if it was mentioned it was after the event, and it's not an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. I was just making sure of that because [Microphone not activated] in passing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, how long will your cross-examination of Mr. Zyrapi be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult to tell. It's fairly lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: More than the rest of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No doubt about that. Right --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I would like to mention to you is that I think this is one of those instances contemplated in your order of where we will ask a little bit of additional time. I can't say for sure that we will, but what I'm concerned about is I don't want to cut short some cross-examination that I think is critical just out of fear that I'll be taking time away from those that are behind me. And if we use additional time, I don't think it will be very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think what we should do is deal with the way in which the evidence of Mr. Tanic is to be presented. Now, are you in a position to deal with that or does it mean summoning someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Your Honour. I would have to deal with it if it's going to be raised now. Mr. Hannis is more aware of other issues but he has had to leave because of personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be done just now. It would have been, I thought, convenient for him. But if it's preferable that he deals with it and that has to be tomorrow, then we'll leave it until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that your preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, we shall have Mr. Zyrapi back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue, a bit later than we had hoped, but we'll hear evidence for about half an hour or so, and the first counsel to deal with evidence today will be Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You will recall that yesterday we were trying to get some good sense of where the Berisa mountains were located in relation to one of your maps, which is P2447. And the first thing I want to make sure that we are clear about is the Berisa mountains is a place that you talked about as being a place where the KLA had headquarters and quite a few of its troops were -- were in those mountains. That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you talked about yesterday when this action was going on in the area of the A, B, and C on your map P2447, and the KLA was withdrawing along with the -- some of the civilian population. You were withdrawing into this area of the Berisa mountains, and that's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is have you be able to see on your screen Prosecution Exhibit 615 and page 23 thereof. And the usher will give you a pen that you can draw on the exhibit with and we'll do a -- make a little exhibit, if we can. Now, what we're going to need to do is zoom in to the proper area, and it is above Suva Reka, between Suva Reka and Malisevo and to the kind of -- almost in the middle. Up a little higher. Try to zoom right in to that area; I think that's where we want to be. Do you see the area that we were talking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what I would like you to do if you can do it on this map -- because I think it's a little better -- I think it's a little better in terms of the -- you can kind of see the green there that's mountains. Could you take a pen and just draw a line around, like encircle, the Berisa mountains for us so we will know where they are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, if you could please be sure to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am drawing a line around Berisha mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we raise the map up just a little bit so we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can't move it once you start drawing on it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, that's right, Judge, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not good enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's probably good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the only other thing I'd like you to do is when you were moving from area B to area C on P2447, can you just draw a line with an arrow maybe on it pointing to the direction that you moved and where you went in this Berisa mountain area. I don't know whether you can do that or not, but if you can I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The movement from B to C, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Basically into the Berisa mountain areas, from Velenica, I guess, maybe in that area.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's probably the best we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'll ask that that be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, but Mr. Marcussen is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would just suggest that we just make sure on the record that the witness drew from the south in a northerly direction, as there is no arrow on the end of the line so we can understand it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this movement you have shown on this map, this occurred I think the 1st or 2nd of April. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This movement occurred on the 31st of March and 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. We're finished with that now. There was a time right after the war, I know, when Bernard Kouchner appointed you to some kind of a position, a co-director or something like that. Can you tell us what that was you were appointed to at that time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In August 2000 I was appointed an associate director of the department for emergency management; that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And basically what were the duties that you had in that department?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of our duties were to develop this department, to administrate the TMK, and to develop emergency units in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And remind me what the TMK is.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Kosova Protection Corps, KPC.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you don't continue to hold that position; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I hold a different post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you comfortable with telling us what it is you do now, what that post is?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a department for management with emergencies. The fire service and the municipalities which are in the process of formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if -- is that -- does that give you a status that would give you sort of automatic access to these archives that you told us about yesterday; and if not, how is it that you got access to these archives?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an access to these archives, not because of my post but also because I knew people who worked in KPS, and that's how I managed to obtain some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: KPC, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And tell us what KPC is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've just had it, the Kosovo Protection Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, we already did that. It was TMK a little while ago. It's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's different language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when Mr. Sepenuk was asking you questions about these archives and the documents that you got from those archives, this kind of an exchange occurred. The question you asked was -- that was asked of you: "Did the Prosecutor's office ask you to obtain this record and records like this?" Your answer was: "They did not ask me directly, but they told me what I could testify about when I came here. "Q. And what was that? What was that conversation? When you say they told you what you could testify about, when was that? When did they tell you that, and what is it they said you could testify about?" Your answer was: "I said this earlier, this was before I came here when I gave my statement in July." And then the question: "If I'm not mistaken, the Prosecution told you what you could testify about. Could you be just a little bit more precise about that. What was conversation with the Prosecution? "A. Well, the Prosecution talked with me about things that I knew that I could testify about. They didn't tell me what to say here. They asked me what I knew and come and tell the truth here." And then this question: "Did they ask you to find records of disciplinary actions by either a local commander or a military court against KLA soldiers who had either murdered or abducted Serbian civilians or alleged Albanian collaborationists? "A. They said in general if I had any documents that I could find, documents that could be useful. They did not specify what kinds of documents." Now, that was kind of a long lead-up, but I think it was important to establish the context. What did you understand to be documents that could be useful?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say "useful," just documents that I can offer as part of my statement. This is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I've -- I've quoted your testimony, the exact words that appear in our transcript. And what it says was: "They said if you had documents you could find, documents that could be useful." How did you decide as you went through these archives what documents you should produce and what documents you should not? What criteria did you use in that regard?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use any criteria. It is just documents that I could find in the mentioned archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have the impression that there are many, many documents in these archives. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many documents there are, but these are the documents that I could find in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about describing the archives. Physically, what do these archives look like? Are there giant boxes full of things or are there cabinets full of documents? How are they arranged? What do they look like?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot fully describe the archives. It's rooms where documents are kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how are they kept? Are they kept in binders or boxes or what?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there was a -- an exhibit that was shown to you yesterday. I don't recall the number of it right now, but it was one of the -- one of the documents that you brought that was an order regarding reports that were to be prepared by commanders, daily combat reports, one in the morning and one in the evening, from each of these groups. I would assume that those daily combat reports are all in those archives somewhere. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should be there, but when I was looking for these documents I couldn't find everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't bring everything that you saw in the archives, did you?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw in the archives, I brought it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in this room -- you described this room full of documents that are in binders and you brought, what, 20 documents. Is that all there were in that room? That's not even one binder worth.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the entire archives that you told us about yesterday consist of less than one binder of documents?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, what I could find I brought here. Maybe there are more documents in that archives but I couldn't find everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, just for a moment could you look at P2463. Can you remember finding that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was found in the archives of Pashtrik Operative Zone. It is in the archives of the second zone of KPC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it in a binder on its own or was it mixed in with other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but not all pertaining to war. There were other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you come to select this one from that particular binder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found other documents in this archive as well, not only this one. And I've submitted many other documents to the Tribunal's office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But how did you decide which ones to select from the binders and which ones to leave in the binders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority of documents, especially in this archive, what I was able to find I brought it to the OTP office in Pristina, to the extent that I could find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can you give us any indication of the volume of documents you've taken to the OTP office in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many documents there were, but there were quite a lot, especially from the Pashtrik Operational Zone. I don't know the exact number, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would have to put one question to the witness to be sure that I answer correctly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what -- no, just tell me your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My understanding is that it is a bundle of 85 or a hundred pages or something like that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, does that sound like the number of documents you handed to the office in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, approximately, that is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not sure I've helped very much, but it's back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is that all of the -- you took then to the office in Pristina all of the archives that you could find?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the documents I could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if any of us went looking at the archives of the KLA, we wouldn't see any documents other than the ones which you turned over to the OTP office in Pristina. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, documents that I could find; I did not say whether there were other documents or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what was the search --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Ackerman. We have Mr. Marcussen on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has said that he went through the entire archives. I'm not sure the basis for -- it looks like Mr. Ackerman is suggesting that there would be no other documents there because the witness has said that he had sorted through every single document in the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only distinction I have in my mind at the moment is between documents which relate to the war and documents which don't relate to the war. But apart from that I haven't heard a distinction, so I don't see anything wrong with the questions. Carry on, please, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, and I haven't got all the references, but you were asked about various documents, when they were shown to you, and you would say, Well, those came from the General Staff archives. And then another document would be shown to you and you would say that came from the Pastrik zone archives. And another one would be shown you and that came from some other archive. And you'll have to forgive me for getting the impression that you were looking at a lot of different archives, not just one. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that yesterday I mentioned that I checked with the archives of the General Staff and of the zones and to see where I could find these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you go to each one yourself or did you rely on someone else providing material from the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some I went myself, and for some others I asked colleagues who worked there for a favour and -- but in most of the cases I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
